chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.summary: The first written records for the history of France appeared in the Iron Age. What is now France made up the bulk of the region known to the Romans as Gaul.

events.label: 2nd c. BC
events.text: The Roman Republic annexed southern Gaul in the late 2nd century BC, and legions under Julius Caesar conquered the rest of Gaul in the Gallic Wars of 58–51 BC.

The medieval Kingdom of France emerged from the western part of Charlemagne's Carolingian Empire, known as West Francia, and achieved increasing prominence under the rule of the House of Capet, founded in 987.
The monarchy initially wielded only limited authority, but Philip II of France brought the Angevin Empire to an end by defeating a coalition of his rivals at the Battle of Bouvines in 1214.
The war ended with a Valois victory in 1453, strengthening French nationalism and increasing the power and reach of the French monarchy.

events.label: 16th c.
events.text: A burgeoning worldwide colonial empire was established in the 16th century.

events.label: 18th c.
events.text: In the late 18th century the monarchy and associated institutions were overthrown in the French Revolution.
The country was governed as a Republic, until Napoleon's French Empire was declared in 1804.

Following his defeat in the Napoleonic Wars, France went through regime changes, being ruled as a monarchy, then Second Republic, then Second Empire, until a more lasting French Third Republic was established in 1870.
France during World War II was one of the Allied Powers but was conquered by Nazi Germany in 1940.
Into the 1960s most of the French colonial empire became independent, while smaller parts were incorporated into the French state as overseas departments and collectivities.

chapters.narrative: The first written records for the history of France appeared in the Iron Age, when what is now France made up the bulk of the region known to the Romans as Gaul [S1]. The Roman Republic annexed southern Gaul in the late 2nd century BC and legions under Julius Caesar conquered the rest in the Gallic Wars of 58–51 BC [S1]. The medieval Kingdom of France emerged from West Francia, the western part of Charlemagne's Carolingian Empire, and achieved prominence under the House of Capet founded in 987 [S1]. A worldwide colonial empire was established in the 16th century, the monarchy was overthrown in the French Revolution in the late 18th century and Napoleon's Empire was declared in 1804, and most of the colonial empire became independent in the 1960s [S1]. These excerpts reflect only a French state-centered perspective [S1].

chapters.title: Prehistory
chapters.summary: Stone tools discovered at Chilhac and Lézignan-la-Cèbe indicate that pre-human ancestors may have been present in France at least 1.6 million years ago. Neanderthals were present in Europe from about 400,000 BC but died out about 40,000 years ago, possibly out-competed by modern humans during a period of cold weather.

events.label: 800 BC
events.text: In 800 BC, Ionian Greeks founded the colony of Massalia (present-day Marseille) on the shores of the Mediterranean Sea, making it one of the oldest cities in France.

events.label: 3rd c. BC
events.text: In the early 3rd century BC, some Belgae (Germani cisrhenani) conquered the surrounding territories of the Somme in northern Gaul after battles supposedly against the Armoricani (Gauls) near Ribemont-sur-Ancre and Gournay-sur-Aronde, where sanctuaries were found.

events.label: 122 BC
events.text: It was this Gaulish participation that caused Provence to be annexed in 122 BC by the Roman Republic.
In the decade following Valerian's capture by the Persians in 260, Postumus established a short-lived Gallic Empire, which included the Iberian Peninsula and Britannia.

events.label: 4th c.
events.text: A migration of Celts occurred in the 4th century in Armorica.
Those same Goths had sacked Rome in 410 and established a capital in Toulouse.
In 418 the Aquitanian province was given to the Goths in exchange for their support against the Vandals.
The Burgundians were resettled by Aëtius near Lugdunum in 443.
The conflict climaxed in 451 at the Battle of Châlons, in which the Romans and Goths defeated Attila.

chapters.narrative: Stone tools discovered at Chilhac and Lézignan-la-Cèbe indicate that pre-human ancestors may have been present in France at least 1.6 million years ago [S2]. Neanderthals were present in Europe from about 400,000 BC but died out about 40,000 years ago, possibly out-competed by modern humans during a period of cold weather [S2]. In 800 BC, Ionian Greeks founded the colony of Massalia on the shores of the Mediterranean Sea, making it one of the oldest cities in France [S2]. Provence was annexed in 122 BC by the Roman Republic due to Gaulish participation [S2]. In 451 at the Battle of Châlons the Romans and Goths defeated Attila [S2]. The excerpts reflect only a Greco-Roman centred point of view [S2].

chapters.title: Frankish kingdoms (486–987)
chapters.summary: In 486 Clovis I, leader of the Salian Franks, defeated Syagrius at Soissons and subsequently united most of northern and central Gaul under his rule. Clovis then recorded a succession of victories against other Germanic tribes such as the Alamanni at Tolbiac.

events.text: Clovis made Paris his capital and established the Merovingian dynasty but his kingdom did not survive his death in 511.
After a last brief reunification (884–887), the imperial title ceased to be held in the western realm, which was to form the basis of the future French kingdom.
Thanks to Abbot Suger's political advice, King Louis VII (junior king 1131–37, senior king 1137–80) enjoyed greater moral authority over France than his predecessors.
When in 1620 the Huguenots proclaimed a constitution for the 'Republic of the Reformed Churches of France', the chief minister Cardinal Richelieu invoked the entire powers of the state to stop it.
The terms for the peace inflicted upon the Spanish kingdoms in the Treaty of the Pyrenees (1659) were harsh, as France annexed Northern Catalonia.
War broke out again between France and the Dutch Republic in the Franco-Dutch War (1672–78).
In 1733 another war broke in central Europe, this time about the Polish succession, and France joined the war against the Austrian Empire.
Peace was settled in the Treaty of Vienna (1738), according to which France would annex, through inheritance, the Duchy of Lorraine.

Having lost its colonial empire, France saw a good opportunity for revenge against Britain in signing an alliance with the Americans in 1778, and sending an army and navy that turned the American Revolution into a world war.
The war was concluded by the Treaty of Paris (1783); the United States became independent.

chapters.narrative: In 486 Clovis I, leader of the Salian Franks, defeated Syagrius at Soissons and subsequently united most of northern and central Gaul under his rule, later recording victories against the Alamanni at Tolbiac [S3]. In 511 Clovis made Paris his capital and established the Merovingian dynasty but his kingdom did not survive his death in 511 [S3]. After a last brief reunification (884–887), the imperial title ceased to be held in the western realm, which was to form the basis of the future French kingdom [S3]. Thanks to Abbot Suger's political advice, King Louis VII enjoyed greater moral authority over France than his predecessors [S3]. The provided excerpts reflect only a Western political perspective focused on French rulers and thus present a limited point of view [S3].

chapters.title: Revolutionary France (1789–1799)
chapters.summary: The French Revolution was a period of political and societal change in France that began with the Estates General of 1789, and ended with the coup of 18 Brumaire in November 1799 and the formation of the French Consulate. Many of its ideas are considered fundamental principles of liberal democracy, while its values and institutions remain central to modern French political discourse.

events.text: The French Revolution was a period of political and societal change in France that began with the Estates General of 1789, and ended with the coup of 18 Brumaire in November 1799 and the formation of the French Consulate.
Military defeats following the outbreak of the French Revolutionary Wars in April 1792 resulted in the insurrection of 10 August 1792.
The monarchy was abolished and replaced by the French First Republic in September, while Louis XVI was executed in January 1793.
About 16,000 people were executed in a Reign of Terror, which ended in July 1794.
Weakened by external threats and internal opposition, the Republic was replaced in 1795 by the Directory.
Four years later in 1799, the Consulate seized power in a military coup led by Napoleon Bonaparte.

chapters.narrative: The French Revolution was a period of political and societal change in France that began with the Estates General of 1789 and ended with the coup of 18 Brumaire in November 1799 and the formation of the French Consulate [S4]. Military defeats following the outbreak of the French Revolutionary Wars in April 1792 resulted in the insurrection of 10 August 1792 [S4]. The monarchy was abolished and replaced by the French First Republic in September, while Louis XVI was executed in January 1793 [S4]. About 16,000 people were executed in a Reign of Terror, which ended in July 1794 [S4]. Weakened by external threats and internal opposition, the Republic was replaced in 1795 by the Directory [S4]. Four years later in 1799, the Consulate seized power in a military coup led by Napoleon Bonaparte [S4].

chapters.title: Napoleonic France (1799–1815)
chapters.summary: As Great Britain was still at war with France, a plan was made to take Egypt from the Ottoman Empire, a British ally. This was Napoleon's idea and the Directory agreed to the plan in order to send the popular general away from the mainland.

events.text: The Revolution in the 1790s abolished the traditional universities.
Napoleon defeated the Ottoman forces during the Battle of the Pyramids (1798).
The Austrian army was defeated at the Battle of Marengo and the Battle of Hohenlinden in 1800.

While at sea, the French had some success at Boulogne, but Nelson's Royal Navy destroyed an anchored Danish and Norwegian fleet at the Battle of Copenhagen (1801), because the Scandinavian kingdoms opposed the British blockade of France.
In 1804, Napoleon was titled Emperor by the senate, thus founding the First French Empire.
There the Russian Empire was defeated at the Battle of Friedland (14 June 1807).

chapters.summary: The century after the fall of Napoleon I was politically unstable: Every [French] head of state from 1814 to 1873 spent part of his life in exile. Every regime was the target of assassination attempts of a frequency that put Spanish and Russian politics in the shade.

events.text: The period from 1789 to 1914, dubbed the "Long nineteenth century" by the historian Eric Hobsbawm, extends from the French Revolution's aftermath to the brink of World War I.

events.label: 19th c.
events.text: The 19th century saw France expanding to nearly its modern territorial limits through annexations and overseas imperialism, notably in Algeria, Indochina, and Africa.

The Second Empire (1852–1870) sought modernization through infrastructure projects like the railway system, yet Napoleon III's foreign policy ventures often ended in failure, notably the catastrophic Franco-Prussian War which led to his capture and deposition.

chapters.title: Colonial empire
chapters.summary: The second colonial empire constituted the overseas colonies, protectorates and mandate territories that came under French rule from the 16th century onward. A distinction is generally made between the "first colonial empire", that existed until 1814, by which time most of it had been lost, and the "second colonial empire", which began with the conquest of Algiers in 1830.

events.label: 16th c.
events.text: The second colonial empire constituted the overseas colonies, protectorates and mandate territories that came under French rule from the 16th century onward.

A distinction is generally made between the "first colonial empire", that existed until 1814, by which time most of it had been lost, and the "second colonial empire", which began with the conquest of Algiers in 1830.
Republicans, at first hostile to empire, only became supportive when Germany after 1880 started to build their own colonial empire.
The damages caused by the war amounted to about 113% of the GDP of 1913, chiefly the destruction of productive capital and housing.
By 1915 the war economy went into high gear, as millions of French women and colonial men replaced the civilian roles of many of the 3 million soldiers.
Famous battles in France include the Battle of Verdun and the Battle of the Somme in 1916, and five separate conflicts called the Battle of Ypres (from 1914 to 1918).
Germany's invasion of Poland in 1939 finally caused France and Britain to declare war against Germany.
Vichy France was established on 10 July 1940 to govern the unoccupied part of France and its colonies.
The French Constitution of 27 October 1946 (Fourth Republic), established the French Union which endured until 1958.
The second colonial empire came to an end after the loss in later wars of Vietnam (1954) and Algeria (1962), and relatively peaceful decolonizations elsewhere after 1960.

chapters.title: Since 1945
chapters.summary: The political scene in 1944–45 was controlled by the Resistance, but it had numerous factions. Charles de Gaulle and the Free France element had been based outside France, but now came to dominate, in alliance with the Socialists, the Christian Democrats (MRP), and what remained of the Radical party.

events.text: The debts left over from World War I, whose payment had been suspended since 1931, were renegotiated in the Blum-Byrnes agreement of 1946.
On 13 October 1946, a new constitution established the Fourth Republic.
France received additional aid from 1951 to 1955 in order to help the country in its war in Indochina.

Pierre France next came to an agreement with Habib Bourguiba, the nationalist leader in Tunisia, for the independence of that colony by 1956, and began discussions with Moroccan nationalists for a French withdrawal.
The May 1958 seizure of power in Algiers by French army units and French settlers opposed to concessions in the face of Arab nationalist insurrection ripped apart the unstable Fourth Republic.
The Algerian War was concluded with the Évian Accords in 1962 which led to Algerian independence.
In 1990, France, led by Mitterrand, joined the short successful Gulf War against Iraq; the French participation to this war was called the Opération Daguet.
Jacques Chirac was reelected in 2002, and became a fierce opponent of the Iraq invasion.
In the 2017 election for president the winner was Emmanuel Macron, the founder of a new party "La République En Marche!" (later Renaissance RE).
In the 2022 presidential election president Macron was re-elected after beating his far-right rival, Marine Le Pen, in the runoff.
